newsitem.title: GERMANY: German builders look poised for strike over pay.
newsitem.headline: German builders look poised for strike over pay.

text.p: German construction workers appeared to be heading into strike action on Monday as the main wages commission of the sector's leading union met to decide whether to accept an arbitrator-brokered pay deal.
Despite pleas from government officials not to strike, the commission seemed likely to reject the arbitration deal, which was approved by a small majority in the arbitration committee.

Officials from several regional units of the IG Bauen-Agrar-Umwelt (IG Bau) union signalled at the weekend that they were unhappy with the deal, which proposed cutting workers' pay by 20 percent during the first three weeks of sickness.
The deal also recommended raising wages by 1.3 percent from last April 1 and reducing Christmas bonuses. German inflation stands at about 1.5 percent.
The IG Bau union had, among other demands, called for wage increase of 2.9 percent and continued full pay during sick leave while employers sought to keep pay unchanged.
Union officials particularly disliked the cutbacks in sick pay and the Christmas bonus. Government officials have urged the union and employers to accept the deal.

Construction minister Klaus Toepfer warned on Friday that a strike would be "poison" for the troubled sector. He noted that new building orders in Germany had fallen by 8.7 percent in January and February.
Labour minister Norbert Bluem also warned of the potentially devastating consequences for the sector of a strike in view of the current weakness in the construction industry.
The decision made by the main wages commission on Monday will pass to the union's board for a final decision on whether to reject or accept the deal.
If the deal is not approved by May 21, the IG Bau union can lawfully call industrial action. The union's wages commission will hold a news conference at 1200 GMT.

Analysts believe any strike is likely to be limited since neither side can afford a prolonged dispute in a sector suffering from mass unemployment, with about 400,000 of its 1.3 million workers out of a job.
